specAnchors.text: draw the main components of the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram (HR diagram)

primer.text: The HR diagram plots luminosity against surface temperature — with temperature running backwards, hottest on the left. Its main band is the main sequence; white dwarfs sit below it, red giants above right, red supergiants above those. Read the corners and every star class falls into place.

modules.title: Reading the HR diagram
modules.opening: The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram plots luminosity on the y-axis (usually in solar units, Sun = 1) against surface temperature on the x-axis, which runs backwards — hot on the left, cool on the right. Most stars lie on the main sequence band from top left to bottom right; white dwarfs sit below it, red giants above its right end, and red supergiants directly above the giants.
keyPoints: The HR diagram plots luminosity (y-axis) against surface temperature (x-axis).
Surface temperature is plotted backwards, hottest on the left, coolest on the right.
Most stars lie on the main sequence band from top left to bottom right.
White dwarfs sit below the main sequence; red giants above its right side; red supergiants above the giants.
The hottest brightest stars are large main sequence stars; the coolest brightest are red supergiants.

low.restatement: Luminosity up the side, temperature backwards along the bottom, and a diagonal main sequence band.
low.analogy: A map of a city at night: the diagonal avenue (main sequence) carries most of the lights, with quiet side streets (white dwarfs) and a bright red district (supergiants).
low.examPointer: Draw the reversed x-axis first — forgetting the temperature inversion is the classic error.

medium.restatement: Region-by-region: band diagonal, dwarfs below-left, giants above-right, supergiants above them.
medium.analogy: A seating plan: the crowd on the diagonal, VIPs glowing above, quiet corners below.
medium.examPointer: Practise drawing the four labelled regions from memory — the spec asks you to draw the main components.

modules.title: Plotting stars on the HR diagram
modules.opening: Plotting on the HR diagram is a two-step lookup: convert the star's luminosity into solar units (the Sun's luminosity is 1, so 10 000 times the Sun is 10⁴), then find the surface temperature on the reversed axis and mark the crossing point.
keyPoints: The Sun's luminosity is 1 in solar units.
A star 10 000 times the Sun's luminosity is plotted at 10⁴.
Locate the surface temperature on the reversed x-axis, then the luminosity on the y-axis.
Mark and label the plotted point where the two values cross.

low.restatement: Convert to solar units, find the reversed-axis temperature, mark the crossing.
low.analogy: Grid references: read along the bottom (temperature, backwards) then up the side (luminosity).
low.examPointer: The Sun = 1 convention turns '10 000 times the Sun' into a clean 10⁴ — show that multiplication in your working.

medium.restatement: Plotting is arithmetic plus orientation: 10⁴ solar units, 20 000 K, upper main sequence.
medium.analogy: Dropping a pin on a map: coordinates first, label afterwards.
medium.examPointer: Label the plotted star — unlabelled points lose the mark.

glossary.definition: The diagonal band on the HR diagram where most stars, including the Sun, lie.
Luminosity units on the HR diagram with the Sun defined as 1.
The hot, dim region below the main sequence on the HR diagram.

workedExample.prompt: On an HR diagram, where do regions A (below the main sequence, left), B (the diagonal band), C (top right) and D (above the band's right end) lie, and where is a star of 20 000 K and 10⁴ solar luminosities plotted?
steps: Identify region A as the white dwarf stars, below and slightly left of the main sequence.
Identify region B as the main sequence band itself, from top left to bottom right.
Identify region C as the red supergiants and region D as the red giants above the band's right end.
Convert the luminosity: 10 000 × 1 = 10 000 = 10⁴ solar units, then locate 20 000 K on the reversed axis and plot the point.
workedExample.finalAnswer: A = white dwarfs, B = main sequence, C = red supergiants, D = red giants; Star X plots at 20 000 K and 10⁴ solar luminosity on the upper main sequence.
